To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
being married is a risk factor for poor psychological responses in men with cancer.

unmarried men with cancer have significantly higher levels of depression, anxiety, anger, confusion and fatigue, and lower levels of positive mood than married men with cancer; and that men with cancer and their wives' support show higher levels of fighting-spirit than men with cancer and wives without support.

being married may be an important protective factor in reducing psychological distress of male cancer patients, and that being married may also be an important factor in promoting fighting spirit among male cancer patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of marital status and spousal support in men and women with cancer.
the relationship between the marital status and the psychological distress in male cancer patients, and the role of marital support.
the role of marital status and marital support for psychological responses to cancer in men.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
marital status is a risk factor for men but not for women, and that marital support is a protective factor for men with cancer but not for women.
the lack of marital support is an independent risk factor for psychological stress and poor coping in male cancer patients.

being married may be beneficial to men with cancer, but not women, in reducing psychological distress, and being unmarried may be detrimental to men with cancer but not women, with respect to psychological distress and fighting spirit.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
men with cancer may be particularly sensitive to the impact of being single or married and to the presence or absence of spousal care and support on their psychological responses to cancer.
being married may be a protective factor for men with cancer, whereas being married may not be a protective factor or a risk factor for women with cancer.
the presence of a supportive spouse may be particularly important for married men, but not married women.
The main takeaway from our work is that
men with cancer who are not married or do not have a supportive spouse may have higher levels of psychological and emotional distress and less ability to fight their illness.
men who are unmarried may be at higher risk for poor psychological outcomes than married men with cancer, which may be related to the lack of marital support.
men with cancer who are married have lower psychological distress and higher fighting spirit than those who are unmarried.
